Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Working Memory Development: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Analyses of Primary School Children in an Adaptive Learning Environment

text.text: The present study investigated the spatial working memory (WM) ability and its developmental change, utilizing large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data from an adaptive learning environment.

Approximately 16% of Dutch primary school children participated in a spatial serial recall task between 2019 and 2025, providing dense, continuous measurements of the same children in their regular educational environment.
Cross-sectional analyses demonstrated the increase of working memory capacity between the ages of six and twelve on average by one item.
However, the spatial complexity of the lists affected this capacity increase.
Moreover, longitudinal analyses of accuracy demonstrated WM ability maturation over time, yet there was no impact of practicing the task.
Furthermore, significant individual differences were observed among children.
Future studies should focus on a better assessment of spatial complexity and the underlying sources for individual differences in WM development.
Working memory (WM) is a mental system that holds information available for processing (Logie & Cowan, 2015).
text.formatted: Working memory (WM) is a mental system that holds information available for processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Logie & Cowan, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, WM is a key component of higher-level cognitive functioning.
Depending on the type of information being processed, WM can be divided into different domains (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; Shah & Miyake, 1996).
text.formatted: Depending on the type of information being processed, WM can be divided into different domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baddeley & Hitch, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Shah & Miyake, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: One of these is spatial WM, which involves maintaining and manipulating information temporarily about the location of objects and their spatial relations.
It is generally assumed that WM abilities develop over the course of childhood (Cowan, 2023; Waterman, Atkinson, & Allen, 2026).
text.formatted: It is generally assumed that WM abilities develop over the course of childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cowan, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Waterman, Atkinson, & Allen, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Throughout this development, there is a large body of evidence supporting the relationship between WM ability and other cognitive abilities such as math, spatial reasoning, and academic performance (Allen, Giofrè, Higgins, & Adams, 2021; Allen, Higgins, & Adams, 2019; Alloway & Alloway, 2010).
text.formatted: Throughout this development, there is a large body of evidence supporting the relationship between WM ability and other cognitive abilities such as math, spatial reasoning, and academic performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen, Giofrè, Higgins, & Adams, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Allen, Higgins, & Adams, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alloway & Alloway, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The purpose of the current study is to assess how spatial WM ability develops.
To do so, we employ a large scale dataset from a real-life learning tool using cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses.
One important aspect of WM ability is WM capacity, which represents the number of items that can be accessed in WM at any given time (Cowan, 2001).
text.formatted: One important aspect of WM ability is WM capacity, which represents the number of items that can be accessed in WM at any given time <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cowan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: WM capacity is limited and increases over childhood, even when accounting for increase in knowledge, the ability to allocate attention, and strategy (Cowan, 2023).
text.formatted: WM capacity is limited and increases over childhood, even when accounting for increase in knowledge, the ability to allocate attention, and strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cowan, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This finding may indicate that in addition to refining cognitive abilities as a whole, children may experience maturation of WM capacity (Cowan, 2016).
text.formatted: This finding may indicate that in addition to refining cognitive abilities as a whole, children may experience maturation of WM capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowan, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Measuring WM capacity, however, is not simple.
First, there is no consensus on what the best measure of WM capacity is (Reynolds, Niileksela, Gignac, & Sevillano, 2022).
text.formatted: First, there is no consensus on what the best measure of WM capacity is <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Reynolds, Niileksela, Gignac, & Sevillano, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Typical measures rely on the set size at which a child answers a list correctly (Cowan, 2016; Finch, 2019). Reynolds et al. (2022) compared different scoring measures with varying levels of strictness and concluded that they measured verbal WM development equally well.
text.formatted: Typical measures rely on the set size at which a child answers a list correctly <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowan, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Finch, 2019)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Reynolds et al. (2022)</ref> compared different scoring measures with varying levels of strictness and concluded that they measured verbal WM development equally well.

text.text: Second, the design of the WM task affects measures of WM capacity.
For example, in visuo-spatial WM tasks, the spatiotemporal structure of a list can facilitate the recall of more items, hence inflating WM capacity measures.

Consecutive items that are in the same row, column, or diagonal of a grid are more likely to be recalled correctly than if they do not share any spatial characteristics (Bor, Duncan, Wiseman, & Owen, 2003; De Lillo, Kirby, & Poole, 2016; Magen & Emmanouil, 2019).
text.formatted: Consecutive items that are in the same row, column, or diagonal of a grid are more likely to be recalled correctly than if they do not share any spatial characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bor, Duncan, Wiseman, & Owen, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">De Lillo, Kirby, & Poole, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Magen & Emmanouil, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: There are recent studies that incorporate spatial chunking and stimulus complexity in adults (De Sardenberg Schmid & Hardiess, 2024; Huang, Ke, Li, Liu, & Ming, 2025); however, the operationalization of spatial chunking is often not clearly specified.
text.formatted: There are recent studies that incorporate spatial chunking and stimulus complexity in adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(De Sardenberg Schmid & Hardiess, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huang, Ke, Li, Liu, & Ming, 2025)</ref>; however, the operationalization of spatial chunking is often not clearly specified.

text.text: Furthermore, in children, a small number of studies have examined the effects of spatial complexity in spatial serial recall tasks (Nutley, Söderqvist, Bryde, Humphreys, & Klingberg, 2009; Zhang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, in children, a small number of studies have examined the effects of spatial complexity in spatial serial recall tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Nutley, Söderqvist, Bryde, Humphreys, & Klingberg, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, it was not clear how spatial chunking was defined in these studies.
In sum, measuring WM capacity is not straightforward.
When measuring WM capacity in spatial WM tasks, it is necessary to define an appropriate quantification for the spatial complexity of the items within a list.
Within the area of WM development, recent studies have utilized large-scale data but much of the empirical work is cross-sectional (e.g., Waterman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Within the area of WM development, recent studies have utilized large-scale data but much of the empirical work is cross-sectional (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Waterman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That is, WM ability is assessed for children of different ages at the same time.
The advantage of this approach is its efficiency.
There are, however, a number of disadvantages.
First, it is difficult to assess the development of WM performance when average scores for all age groups are calculated.
These averages may obscure developmental patterns.
Figure 1A shows a hypothetical example.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref> shows a hypothetical example.

text.text: In this example, WM develops in stages represented by the staircases: With each step in the development, WM capacity increases by one item.
These steps may occur at different times for each child.
The points represent WM capacity measures for different children who experience one of the two possible developmental patterns.
If WM performance is averaged across individuals, stages disappear and development looks linear.
Another issue with this averaging is that individual differences in development, such as between the two underlying developmental patterns, cannot be captured.

There are few examples in the literature that employ longitudinal designs to study WM ability (Ahmed, Ellis, Ward, Chaku, & Davis-Kean, 2022; Lehmann, 2015), mainly focusing on verbal tasks, rather than spatial tasks.
text.formatted: There are few examples in the literature that employ longitudinal designs to study WM ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmed, Ellis, Ward, Chaku, & Davis-Kean, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lehmann, 2015)</ref>, mainly focusing on verbal tasks, rather than spatial tasks.

text.text: The studies showed increases and sometimes nonlinear growth in WM ability.
The key advantage of these longitudinal designs is that they separate within-person change from between-person differences.

However, due to their high cost and logistical demands, longitudinal studies rarely include intensive measurement, and the limited number of observations per occasion makes it difficult to distinguish true WM capacity from day-to-day fluctuations in performance (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: However, due to their high cost and logistical demands, longitudinal studies rarely include intensive measurement, and the limited number of observations per occasion makes it difficult to distinguish true WM capacity from day-to-day fluctuations in performance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: In summary, the typical implementation of cross-sectional and longitudinal designs in the literature has disadvantages: cross-sectional work averages over individuals and longitudinal work samples them too infrequently.
However, to capture true changes in individual WM development, a large number of observations and repeated measurements occasions within children are required.
Our study combines these features by leveraging large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data with repeated observations within children.
The current study has two aims.
First, we aim to investigate different WM capacity measures.
Second, we aim to assess the developmental change of WM capacity and performance.
To achieve these aims we employ large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data from an adaptive spatial recall task.
Adaptive learning environments provide a unique and ecologically valid opportunity to investigate cognitive development in large and diverse samples of children.

In a previous study, we utilized data from this learning environment to replicate several benchmark findings of adults in children for serial recall, including set-size effects (Ertekin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In a previous study, we utilized data from this learning environment to replicate several benchmark findings of adults in children for serial recall, including set-size effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ertekin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This study primarily focused on within-list performance, adaptive ability measures, list difficulty, and error patterns, while the current study focuses on development of capacity and performance.
Our study contributes to the field of WM development in several ways.
First, our dataset is exceptionally large: it includes about 16% of the primary school students in the Netherlands between the 2019 and 2024 school years (Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs, 2026).
Most critically, the dataset offers dense, continuous measurement of the same children over extended periods, yielding around 24 million of observations for 350,000 children.
This measurement density allows us to characterize individual developmental trajectories with far greater resolution than traditional designs.

Second, because the adaptive game calibrates list difficulty to each child's current ability level, it avoids the typical measurement problems of fixed difficulty assessments: If the same items are used for children with very different abilities -either across or within age groups -it is common to observe floor and ceiling effects, or even the disengagement of children who experience the task as too difficult or too easy (Gonthier, Aubry, & Bourdin, 2018).
text.formatted: Second, because the adaptive game calibrates list difficulty to each child's current ability level, it avoids the typical measurement problems of fixed difficulty assessments: If the same items are used for children with very different abilities -either across or within age groups -it is common to observe floor and ceiling effects, or even the disengagement of children who experience the task as too difficult or too easy <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gonthier, Aubry, & Bourdin, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Third, by measuring spatial rather than verbal WM in longitudinal data, we broaden the empirical and methodological basis for WM development.

We approach WM development from two complementary perspectives: cross-sectional for a simple representation of the population-level structure, and longitudinal for a deeper understanding of individual-level dynamics.

First, in the cross-sectional analyses, we evaluate different WM capacity measures in the spatial task and assess relations between school year (grade 1-6) and WM capacity measures in the adaptive system.
We particularly focus on the effect of spatial configuration on this relationship as the spatial structure of a list can support recall and can therefore inflate WM capacity estimates.
Second, we use longitudinal accuracy data to characterize developmental trajectories within individual children, including maturation and practice of the spatial task.

In this type of intense longitudinal data, any improvement in WM performance could be due to natural WM development (i.e., maturation) or to better understanding the setting and rules of the current task.
Therefore, these two forms of performance improvement have to be distinguished.

Our dataset enables us to do this by assessing maturation effects in children with sparse playing behavior over a long period of time and by assessing practice effects in children with intense playing behavior.
Note that because we only use one task, simple practice effects cannot be distinguished from transfer effects (Von Bastian & Oberauer, 2014).
text.formatted: Note that because we only use one task, simple practice effects cannot be distinguished from transfer effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Von Bastian & Oberauer, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Together, the cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses extend previous findings (Ahmed et al., 2022; Reynolds et al., 2022) from the verbal domain to the spatial domain using a more fine grained design.
text.formatted: Together, the cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses extend previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmed et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Reynolds et al., 2022)</ref> from the verbal domain to the spatial domain using a more fine grained design.

text.text: Data were collected from the online adaptive learning platform Prowise Learn (https://www.oefenweb.nl), which focuses on K-12 education.
text.formatted: Data were collected from the online adaptive learning platform Prowise Learn (<ref type="url" target="https://www.oefenweb.nl">https://www.oefenweb.nl</ref>), which focuses on K-12 education.

text.text: Children practice in mathematics and language skills across 57 different learning games.
The learning platform is used in Dutch schools for practice, therefore, the Mole game was not built for specific research questions.
The data from the platform nevertheless provide a means for studying WM development in students' regular practice environment by analyzing millions of responses from thousands of users.
Figure 2 depicts a trial in the "Mole game" ("Mollenspel" in Dutch), a spatial forward serial recall task, used in the present study.
When playing the game, children see a list, that is a sequence of moles (i.e., items) appearing in a grid, varying in 3 × 3, 3 × 4, 3 × 5, 4 × 3, 4 × 4, 4 × 5, 5 × 3, 5 × 4, or 5 × 5 configurations.
The number of moles in a list (set size) varies between 1 and 9.
See Supplement B for the distribution of list characteristics including, set size, grid configurations, and spatial structure.
In the Mole game, lists are presented as sessions of 10 trials where each trial may contain different numbers of moles.
An empty grid is presented throughout a trial and each mole pops up (625 ms), stays still (1000 ms), and backs down (625 ms) in a square of the grid (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: An empty grid is presented throughout a trial and each mole pops up (625 ms), stays still (1000 ms), and backs down (625 ms) in a square of the grid (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: There is no time between the appearances of two consecutive moles, and the same square can be used by more than one mole in a list, and even in immediate succession.
Presented lists are selected by the adaptive system to match the ability of the children.
The children's task is to recall and then indicate the moles' positions by pressing the corresponding squares in the same order.
After indicating the response for the entire trial, which turns squares to blue with the corresponding serial position numbers, they click the "OK" button to submit the response.
If the response is correct, the answer becomes green.
If the response for the trial is incorrect, the response becomes red, and the correct serial positions of the moles in corresponding squares appear.
If children correctly submit all the moles in the trial within a 20-s time frame, they earn coins that can be used to acquire trophies.
As children progress through the session, the coins they collect are seen in blue on the top right of the screen.
The number of coins they earn or lose is related to the accuracy, time it takes for them to respond and the game difficulty they choose.
The adaptivity of the platform relies on the on-the-fly Elo-based estimation algorithm originating from chess (Elo, 1978), where each player has a unique rating reflecting their ability.
text.formatted: The adaptivity of the platform relies on the on-the-fly Elo-based estimation algorithm originating from chess <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Elo, 1978)</ref>, where each player has a unique rating reflecting their ability.

text.text: Differences between expected (based on the ratings) and observed outcomes are used to update the players' ratings.

In Prowise Learn, students do not compete against each other like in chess, but they compete against the lists: The accuracy and speed of a student's response to a list affect both the student's ability rating and the list's difficulty rating.
If a student correctly and swiftly remembers a list, their ability rating increases; if a student answers incorrectly or too slowly, their ability rating decreases.

In contrast to traditional testing methodologies, this dual analytic capability enables the system to not only evaluate a student's ability but also to determine the list difficulty based on playing behavior.
This feature is particularly powerful because it enables researchers to study how the characteristics of the lists contribute to the students' performance.

This self-organizing system does not rely on pilot testing or reference group data, ensuring that adding more lists and participants does not affect the test validity and reliability (Brinkhuis et al., 2018; Klinkenberg, Straatemeier, & van der Maas, 2011).

text.text: Prowise Learn is presented as a gamified practice environment for schools and families.
Children access the platform via schools or family subscription.
Many of the math games are used as practice in class or homework.
The Mole game is one of the games under the Creative Games category of Math Garden (Rekentuin in Dutch) on the platform.
Participation in research is voluntary and those who choose not to participate are excluded from the study.
Participants play the games both at school and at home, deciding for themselves or under the instruction of a teacher when to play, how long to play, and which learning activities to complete.

Data were collected from 357,931 primary school children for the Mole game, from Grade 1 (age around 6-7) to Grade 6 (age around 12), resulting in a total of 23,760,350 trials between 2019 and 2025, which corresponds to about 16% of the children between grades 1 to 6 (Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs, 2026).
Dutch primary education begins at age 4 in Group 1.
We therefore included children in dataset starting from Group 3 (around age 6-7), which roughly corresponds to Grade 1 in many other school systems.
Gender (coded as female/male) was available for only about half of the data and therefore not used to characterize the full sample.
No information on other demographics or socioeconomic characteristics was provided to the researchers.
To assess the data cross-sectionally and longitudinally, analyses were conducted at different levels of the data.
Because we did not design the game ourselves and the data were not collected in a controlled setting, we filtered them before analysis.

text.text: In the game, lists mostly have some level of spatial structure (see Supplement C).
Children may encounter both structured and unstructured lists of the same set size across different sessions.
For example, a child may complete a structured set-size-4 list early in their interaction with the game and later encounter an unstructured set-size-4 list.
If only set size is considered, such differences in structure may obscure meaningful interpretation of WM capacity.
Therefore, next, the effect of spatial structure on WM capacity, and its development was analyzed.
For analyses, we used a combination of Bayes factor tests of independence, Bayesian parameter estimation and Bayesian model comparison with Bayes factors.
For longitudinal analyses, we derived temporal variables to investigate the effects of maturation and practice over years.
Figure 5 depicts how these variables are coded for the first two weeks of an exemplary child.

text.text: The starting age represents the age a child starts playing the game.
We expect better WM performance for older children due to maturation.
In addition, the days since start represents the number of days since a child's first game-play in the data.
As we control for practice over days with the between-day gap variable, days since start represents the maturation and we expect to find a positive effect.
The within-day trial index represents the sequential trial number within a day.
If practice improved children's accuracy, children should become more accurate in later trials as they progress through a day.
Therefore, we would expect a positive effect of this variable.
Alternatively, the adaptive algorithm may account for this practice.
Because children's ability estimation is updated after every trial, a correct answer increases the difficulty of the list in the next trial.
Any gains from practice would then be offset by harder lists, which would lead to no effect of practice.
An alternative explanation is fatigue, if no practice effects are found.
However, the children can stop the game at any time and resume it whenever they want.
Therefore, the effect of fatigue will most likely be minor.
Finally, the between-day gap represents the number of days since the last game-play.
In our data, game-play frequency varies between children.
For example, some children play every other day while others play every other month.
Therefore, smaller between-day gap means more frequent play and practice over days.
If practice improved children's accuracy, we would expect a negative effect of this variable.
In contrast, bigger gaps between game-play correspond to more time for natural maturation in WM.
If maturation is more important than practicing the game, we may find positive effects.
Overall, in this adaptive system, if developmental change reflects only maturation, accuracy should increase with starting age (between-child) and days since start (within-child).
If developmental change reflects only practice, accuracy should increase with within-day trial index, and decrease with between-day gap.

Finally, a mixture of maturation and practice effects would be reflected by positive effects in starting age, days since start and within-day trial index, and depending on which side is stronger we would expect a positive or a negative between-day gap effect.
In this study, we hypothesized that between-child maturation (starting age) and within-child maturation (days since start) would show positive associations with trial-level accuracy.
We further hypothesized that practice-related predictors would show that practice would be less influential than maturation.

Because the algorithm expects increasing performance after correct answers and practice effects may not be strong enough to support this expectation, we predicted that the probability of a correct response should decrease with increasing within-day trial index.
However, between-day gap would show a positive effect on accuracy, consistent with maturation rather than practice benefits.

Because of the computational cost of multilevel models on data of this size in longitudinal analyses, we deviated from the preregistration in two respects.
First, in data selection, the preregistration specified a threshold, which is including lists observed more than 500 times in the whole data set.
As the full dataset includes significantly more children, this threshold allows for the inclusion of lists with too few observations to estimate difficulty reliably.
Therefore, in the full dataset, we included the same lists from the preregistration instead of using the threshold.
The same criterion was applied to the training data.
This allowed models to estimate list difficulty close to observed difficulty.
Second, we preregistered frequentist model comparison and a hierarchical Bayesian final model; we instead used Bayesian estimation with variational inference for both.
We refitted the final model under four random seeds to check the stability of the estimates (Supplement E).

text.text: This test assumes independent observations, which is violated when a child contributes multiple set sizes.
We therefore used the latest trial for each child rather than all trials as specified in the preregistration.
This change did not alter the results and conclusions.
Bayes factor tests of independence compares two models.

Under the null model, the proportion of observations for each last set size is the same in every grade, and, under the alternative model, the proportion of observations for each last set size varies across grades.
Evidence against independence was decisive in all conditions (log 10 BF easy = 668, log 10 BF medium = 936, log 10 BF hard = 1749).
These results suggest that the set size of the lists children engage with tracks developmental differences and may therefore be used as a measure of WM capacity.

To identify an appropriate measure of WM capacity within the adaptive system, we computed Bayes factors (BF) for models predicting children's latest ability rating from different summaries of set size (mean, median, maximum, and 90th percentile), focusing on the hard difficulty setting.

BFs were computed using the generalTestBF function from the BayesFactor package (v0.9.12.4.6) with default priors, comparing each predictor model against an intercept-only model (Morey & Rouder, 2026).

To examine how children's working memory (WM) performance develops over time within the adaptive learning system, trial-level accuracy was modeled using a Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression.
We compared three models' predictive performance to see if inclusion of maturation and practice predictors improved the null model (see Supplement E).
In the final model, accuracy on each trial was regressed on game difficulty, maturation (starting age, days since start), and practice (within-day trial index, between-day gap).
The model included by-child random intercepts and uncorrelated by-child random slopes for days since start, as well as random intercepts for lists.
We verified the stability of parameter estimates across four runs (see Supplement E for the estimation plot and weakly informative priors).
Fixed effects of the model showed a clear between-child maturation effect: children who started older were more accurate (starting age: posterior mean = 0.162, SE = 0.001, 95% CI = [0.159, 0.164]).
There was also within-child maturation over time (days since start: mean = 0.082, SE = 0.003, 95% CI = [0.076, 0.087]).
Within a day, accuracy declined across successive trials (within-day trial index: mean = -0.071, SE = 0.002, 95% CI = [-0.075, -0.066]), showing no practice effect in the adaptive system.

The gap between game-play also supported the absence of a practice effect in the system (between-day gap: mean = 0.015, SE = 0.001, 95% CI = [0.012, 0.017]), indicating that longer gaps led to improved accuracy.
For game difficulty, the effects were either zero or very small across four different seeds.
Random effects revealed substantial variability at both the child and list levels.

Children differed considerably in their baseline ability (SD = 0.471, 95% CI [0.466, 0.475] on the log-odds scale), and also differed in their rate of improvement over game duration (SD = 0.152 [0.151, 0.153]).
Lists also varied in difficulty (SD = 0.244 [0.240, 0.249]).

The present work aimed to assess the development of children's working memory ability, by providing a fine-grained analysis of large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data.
What sets our study apart is using large-scale real-life data from an adaptive learning environment with a spatial serial forward recall task.
Our data are dense and big, equivalent to about 16% of the currently enrolled primary school students in the Netherlands.

Combining the advantages of cross-sectional and longitudinal data analyses, repeated measurements of children over several years allowed us to characterize individual WM development, while distinguishing developmental changes from performance fluctuations.

We conducted a number of cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, assessing our hypotheses that (1.) working memory develops considerably between ages six and twelve, (2.) that the spatial structure affects measurement of WM capacity, and (3.) that there is evidence for maturation of working memory ability within children, and (4.) that practice effects are less pronounced than maturation effects.
In addition, we found considerable individual differences across children, even within the same age group.
The results provided evidence in favor of all of these hypotheses.
With real-life large-scale data, fitting cognitive models of WM capacity is difficult, and tracking accuracy is not straightforward in an adaptive environment.
In the cross-sectional analyses, we therefore asked whether the set size of a list can serve as a proxy for WM capacity.

As Elo-based ability ratings are already established as a psychometric tool for representing WM ability of children (Ertekin et al., 2025; Ven, Maas, Straatemeier, & Jansen, 2013), we used them as a benchmark to select our capacity measure as the mean set size of correctly answered lists among other summary indices.

text.text: Our results, however, showed that recall performance depends not only on set size of the list but also on the spatial configuration of the list.
Relying on set size alone without considering the effect of spatial complexity therefore inflates estimated capacity and, more consequentially, obscures its development.

For highly structured lists, WM capacity estimates were inflated in the youngest children and the developmental differences largely disappeared, whereas unstructured lists showed a clear developmental increase.
When considering the spatial complexity, WM capacity increased gradually across grades replicating studies in the literature, but with diminishing growth toward later grades (ages around 12-13).
These findings imply that WM capacity development cannot be measured independently of the spatial configuration of lists.
We quantified spatial configuration as spatial structure, and we do not claim it includes all spatial information that affects recall.
The existing literature on quantifying spatial configuration or chunking is inconsistent and relies in part on subjective measures (e.g., De Sardenberg Schmid & Hardiess, 2024; Huang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The existing literature on quantifying spatial configuration or chunking is inconsistent and relies in part on subjective measures <ref type="bibr">(e.g., De Sardenberg Schmid & Hardiess, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the candidate spatial variables of a list are strongly intercorrelated, which makes their separate contributions hard to isolate.
It is also not feasible in practice to construct an item bank of a comparable size to ours in which the items of a list stand in no spatial relation to one another.
Therefore, future studies need theoretically motivated work that extends the measurement of spatial WM capacity beyond the number of items recalled to the spatial configuration of these items.

In the longitudinal analyses, we showed that WM performance increases with maturation across primary school by extending studies on verbal WM development (Ahmed et al., 2022; Lehmann, 2015) to spatial WM development.
text.formatted: In the longitudinal analyses, we showed that WM performance increases with maturation across primary school by extending studies on verbal WM development <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmed et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lehmann, 2015)</ref> to spatial WM development.

text.text: Moreover, there was no practice effect in our system.
One key result was the extent of individual differences: children of the same age differ substantially, both in the level and in the rate of development.
Figure 9 provides examples of children who played the game for more than four years.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">9</ref> provides examples of children who played the game for more than four years.

text.text: Some children developed quickly and then stagnated, while others showed more continuous improvement in performance.
Because our data are intensive and span long periods, individual differences are unlikely to only reflect day-to-day fluctuations in performance.
These results suggest that WM development is not a uniform maturation process, and that children may differ in the timing and pace of change.
In addition, the different trajectories and rates suggest that children may reach similar levels through different developmental curves.
What accounts for these differences in development is beyond the scope of the current study.

They may reflect the strategies children use and when they start to use them, especially while encoding spatial complexity of lists, or other child-level factors such as socioeconomic status that we did not analyze.
Furthermore, in our longitudinal analyses, the game difficulty settings had no detectable effect on accuracy.
This contrasts with practice-based games in the system, such as math games for the practice of addition, where difficulty settings do affect performance.
One explanation might be that WM ability is resistant to practice, similar to other stable cognitive abilities (Breit, Scherrer, Tucker-Drob, & Preckel, 2024), while math abilities are more pliable.
text.formatted: One explanation might be that WM ability is resistant to practice, similar to other stable cognitive abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Breit, Scherrer, Tucker-Drob, & Preckel, 2024)</ref>, while math abilities are more pliable.

text.text: Overall, we showed maturation of WM ability in primary school in an adaptive system utilizing cross-sectional analyses, replicating established results, and longitudinal analyses, extending from a verbal task to a spatial task.
These two sets of analyses allowed us to address methodological difficulties and substantive gaps in the WM development literature.

Taken together, they show that with a careful data selection, adaptive learning environments generate data of a scale that laboratory designs rarely achieve, and provide a real-world, externally valid setting to study cognitive development.
